Louis IX. From 1214 to 1270, he was a French king revered for his piety, justice, and military ambition. He led two major crusades and expanded French territory, becoming the ideal of Christian kingship and one of France's most celebrated monarchs. After his death, he was canonized as a saint, the only French king ever to receive that honor.

Pope Boniface VIII canonized him in 1297, cementing his reputation for personal righteousness and moral authority. But long before that, Louis had earned his spiritual stature. He led the Seventh Crusade from 1248 to 1254, sailing east to recapture the Holy Land. The campaign ended in disappointment—he was captured by the Saracens and had to be ransomed for his freedom. Yet he was not discouraged. Late in his life, he launched the Eighth Crusade in 1270, determined to reclaim the holy sites. But he died of plague in Tunis before the mission could take hold.

At home, Louis reformed the French legal system itself. He heard grievances personally from his subjects, sitting under an oak tree at Vincennes. His codification of law and pursuit of impartial justice enhanced the authority of the crown and made royal justice a cornerstone of French governance. In 1239 he acquired the Crown of Thorns relic, the legendary crown placed on Christ's head. He built the magnificent Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house this precious relic, making France a pilgrimage destination for all of Christendom.

Diplomatically, Louis expanded French territory through the Treaty of Paris in 1259 with Henry III of England, confirming French control of Normandy and other contested territories. His long reign from 1226 to 1270 consolidated Capetian power and made France the preeminent medieval Christian kingdom.
